newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: U.N. restricts Sierra Leone travel after ambush.
newsitem.headline: U.N. restricts Sierra Leone travel after ambush.

text.p: The United Nations restricted travel for its workers in Sierra Leone on Wednesday after unidentified gunmen shot a senior U.N. aid official and fatally wounded his driver in an ambush.

U.N. representative Elizabeth Lwanga told Reuters that personnel had been banned from travelling on the road where the vehicle was ambushed late on Tuesday, between the northern town of Makeni and the capital Freetown.
"While it is a setback we hope it is not the way things will develop," Lwanga said. "We were all taken by surprise."
Robert Painter, the American head of the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs in the West African nation, was shot in the foot. The driver, a Sierra Leonean aged 53, died later in hospital.

Around six attackers, some bare-chested, some in combat fatigues or wearing bandanas, sprayed a convoy of two vehicles with automatic arms fire near a village called Madina, 15 miles (25 km) from Makeni and about 90 miles (145 km) from Freetown.

The attack was the first time a U.N. vehicle has been specifically targeted. The road had been safe since before President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh signed a peace deal in November.

"If, as it appears, this was a deliberate ambush on clearly marked U.N. and NGO (non-governmental organisation) vehicles, it could have serious implications for the delivery of humanitarian assistance in Sierra Leone," a U.N. official said.
The motive and identity of the attackers were not immediately clear and the government said it would launch an immediate investigation.

"Even though we have not been able to identify the gunmen we will track them down whether they are Kamajors (hunters), rebels or soldiers who have deserted from the army," presidential adviser Sheka Mansaray told Reuters.

Fighting between the army and the rebels, who took up arms in 1991, has largely ceased but implementation of the deal has dragged and clashes between the army and traditional hunters, their former allies, have complicated peace efforts.

At least 80 bodies were found after weekend fighting between the army and a hunters' militia in the eastern town of Kenema. More than 20 people were killed in two seperate outbreaks of fighting in the north on Sunday and Monday.

Painter, from Chicago, and other officials had been visiting projects in Makeni. Kathy Jones, British deputy head of the U.N. peace operation in Sierra Leone, and a World Bank official were also in the car.
